course.title: Earth and Environmental Science
course.description: From the layers of the planet to its energy balance, weather, oceans, carbon cycle and living systems, with the numbers needed to reason about them.
course.audience: A capable adult with basic maths who has met energy and forces in Discere's physics course and ecosystems in biology. No geology or meteorology assumed.

paragraphs: The deepest hole ever drilled reaches about 12 kilometres into a planet whose radius is 6,371 kilometres, and yet the boundary between Earth's mantle and its core is known to lie about 2,891 kilometres down. Most of what is known about the Earth was found in this way, by reasoning from measurements made at the surface: the times at which earthquake waves reach distant stations, the fraction of an isotope left in a rock, the pressure on a barometer, or the carbon dioxide in a flask of air. Earth and environmental science is the study of the planet as one system, its rock, air, water and life, and of the energy and matter that move between them.

Much of the subject comes down to a few quantities and the arithmetic that links them. The 1,361 watts of sunlight that fall on each square metre facing the Sun, spread over a turning sphere and partly reflected, give the temperature the planet would have without its atmosphere, and the gap between that figure and the measured one is the greenhouse effect. A rate of a few centimetres a year, kept up for millions of years, opens an ocean, and the rise from about 280 parts per million of carbon dioxide before industry to the 421 that NOAA recorded at Mauna Loa in 2023 can be turned into tonnes of carbon and then into a change in the planet's energy balance. Once you can make those links, you can check a claim about the climate, a resource or a landscape against its numbers for yourself.
outcomes: You'll be able to name Earth's layers and explain how earthquake waves showed that the outer core is liquid.
You'll be able to turn a plate speed in centimetres per year into a distance, and classify a rock by how it formed.
You'll be able to date a sample from its half-life and estimate air pressure at a given height.
You'll be able to compute the sunlight Earth absorbs, the temperature that balances it, and the size of the greenhouse effect.
You'll be able to predict wind around a low, find a cloud base, and calculate sea-level rise from added water.
You'll be able to convert carbon units, relate forcing to warming, follow energy through food chains, and work out how long a resource lasts.
introduction.prerequisites: It builds on Physics: Motion and Forces, Biology: Cells to Ecosystems, Maths Foundations.

modules.title: The solid Earth
modules.description: Layers, moving plates, the rock cycle and the clock that dates them.

modules.title: Air, energy and water
modules.description: The atmosphere, the energy it balances, the weather it carries and the oceans that store heat.

modules.title: Climate, life and resources
modules.description: The carbon cycle, what has changed and why, how ecosystems pass energy along, and the limits on what people draw from them.

concepts.title: Earth's layers
concepts.summary: Crust, mantle, liquid outer core and solid inner core, separated by changes in composition and in wave speed.

concepts.title: Seismic evidence
concepts.summary: P waves pass through solids and liquids; S waves pass through solids only, so the S-wave shadow shows a liquid outer core.

concepts.title: Plate boundaries
concepts.summary: Divergent plates move apart, convergent plates collide or one sinks (subduction), transform plates slide past each other.

concepts.title: Plate speed
concepts.summary: Plates move at centimetres per year; 1 cm per year is 10 km per million years.

concepts.title: Three rock families
concepts.summary: Igneous rock cools from melt, sedimentary rock builds from deposited grains, metamorphic rock changes in the solid state under heat and pressure.

concepts.title: Crystal size and cooling
concepts.summary: Slow cooling underground makes large crystals; fast cooling at the surface makes small ones or glass.

concepts.title: Half-life
concepts.summary: The time for half the atoms of a radioactive isotope to decay; after n half-lives the fraction left is (1/2)^n.

concepts.title: Age of Earth
concepts.summary: About 4.54 billion years, from lead isotopes in meteorites and the oldest Earth minerals.

concepts.title: Atmosphere layers
concepts.summary: Troposphere (weather, falls with height), stratosphere (ozone, rises with height), mesosphere, thermosphere.

concepts.title: Pressure and height
concepts.summary: Air pressure falls roughly by half every 5.5 km near the surface, because pressure is the weight of the air above.

concepts.title: Albedo
concepts.summary: The fraction of incoming sunlight a surface or planet reflects; Earth's is about 0.30.

concepts.title: Greenhouse effect
concepts.summary: Gases that absorb and re-emit infrared raise the surface temperature above the temperature a bare planet would have.

concepts.title: Pressure gradient
concepts.summary: Air accelerates from high to low pressure; on a rotating Earth it is deflected to the right in the north and to the left in the south.

concepts.title: Cloud base
concepts.summary: Rising air cools about 9.8 degrees C per km until it reaches its dew point; cloud base is about 125 m per degree of gap between temperature and dew point.

concepts.title: Seawater density
concepts.summary: Cold and salty water is denser; dense water sinks and drives the slow global overturning circulation.

concepts.title: Sea-level arithmetic
concepts.summary: Added volume divided by ocean area gives the rise; thermal expansion of warming water adds to it.

concepts.title: Carbon reservoirs
concepts.summary: The ocean, soils, vegetation, atmosphere and rocks store carbon; fluxes between them differ greatly in speed.

concepts.title: Carbon units
concepts.summary: 1 GtC equals 44/12 GtCO2, and about 2.13 GtC in the atmosphere raises CO2 by 1 ppm.

concepts.title: Radiative forcing
concepts.summary: The change in the energy balance from a cause; for CO2, forcing = 5.35 x ln(C / C0) W/m2.

concepts.title: Climate sensitivity
concepts.summary: The equilibrium warming for a doubling of CO2; the IPCC AR6 best estimate is about 3 degrees C with a likely range of 2.5 to 4.

concepts.title: Trophic efficiency
concepts.summary: Roughly 10 percent of the energy at one level reaches the next, so chains are short.

concepts.title: Carrying capacity
concepts.summary: The population an environment can sustain; logistic growth slows as N approaches K.

concepts.title: Stocks and flows
concepts.summary: A stock changes by inflow minus outflow; a stock falls when use exceeds renewal.

concepts.title: Capacity factor
concepts.summary: Actual energy produced divided by what the plant would produce at full power all year (8,760 hours).

lessons.title: What lies beneath

lead.text: A large earthquake shakes the ground for several minutes, and instruments called **seismometers** around the world record that shaking, so the same event is measured from many directions at once. The waves that cross the interior arrive in two groups. The first to arrive are **P waves**, in which the rock is squeezed and stretched along the direction the wave is travelling, and the second are **S waves**, in which the rock is shaken from side to side, at right angles to that direction.

The two kinds respond differently to what they pass through. A P wave can cross a solid, a liquid or a gas, because all of them can be compressed. An S wave needs a material that resists being sheared, and a liquid does not resist: its layers simply slide past one another. So *S waves travel through solids only*, and an S wave that meets a liquid goes no further.

reveal.text: The next screen shows where the S waves are missing on a cross-section, and which layer is responsible.

lead.text: The figure draws Earth to scale, with an earthquake at the top. In the second view P waves travel through the whole planet, and the ones that cross the core change direction at its boundary, because the waves are slower in the liquid beyond it. That bending turns them away from a ring on the far side where hardly any P waves arrive, a ring called the **P-wave shadow**. In the third view S waves cross the mantle without difficulty, but the rays that would have to pass through the core stop at its edge, which leaves a wider band, called the **S-wave shadow**, where no S waves arrive at all.

Distances over the globe are measured as the angle at Earth's centre between the earthquake and the seismometer, in **degrees of arc**, so the point directly opposite the earthquake is 180 degrees away. The S-wave shadow begins roughly 100 degrees of arc from the earthquake and reaches to that opposite point, while the P-wave shadow runs only from about there to about 140 degrees, beyond which the bent P waves arrive again. Records from many earthquakes showed the same bands every time, and the edges of the bands give the depth of the boundary.

afterFigure.text: The reasoning took several steps and several people. In 1906 Richard Oldham reported that waves crossing the centre of the Earth arrive later than a uniform planet would allow, and he explained this by a core. In 1913 Beno Gutenberg used the shadow to place the core boundary at about 2,900 kilometres, a value now refined to 2,891 kilometres. In 1936 Inge Lehmann found faint P waves arriving inside the P-wave shadow, which could be explained only if the core held a smaller, separate centre, and later work showed that this **inner core** is solid.

diagram.alt: A cross-section of Earth to scale with an earthquake at the top. One view labels crust, mantle, outer core and inner core. One shows P waves crossing the whole planet, bending at the core. One shows S waves stopping at the core, with a heavy arc on the far side where no S waves arrive.

lead.text: Reading from the surface downward, the **crust** is a thin skin of rock, the **mantle** is the thick layer of hot rock beneath it that reaches to 2,891 kilometres, and the **core** is mostly iron and nickel, liquid in its outer part down to 5,150 kilometres and solid in the inner core, whose radius is about 1,220 kilometres. The boundary between the crust and the mantle was found in 1909 by Andrija Mohorovičić, who noticed that waves from an earthquake in Croatia reached distant stations sooner than a uniform crust would allow, because some of them had dipped into the denser mantle and sped up. The boundary still carries his name, the **Moho**.
The crust is not the same everywhere. Oceanic crust is about 7 kilometres thick and made of dark, dense basalt, whereas continental crust averages about 35 kilometres and is made of lighter rock.

afterFigure.text: Even the thicker kind is thin once it is set beside the planet.

reveal.text: The crust is a thin skin, but it is thickest under the continents. Even the deepest borehole, at 12 km, would not have reached the base of average continental crust.

steps.headline: Find the radius of the core from the depth of the core–mantle boundary, which is 2,891 km down.

workedSteps.text: A depth is measured down from the surface and a radius is measured out from the centre, so a depth and the radius at the same place add up to the whole radius of the planet, 6,371 km.
The core reaches from the centre out to the core–mantle boundary, which is 2,891 km down.
Its radius is therefore the whole radius less that depth.
The core is a ball of that radius, a little more than half of the planet's radius.

steps.headline: Do the same for the inner core, whose boundary is 5,150 km down.

workedSteps.text: The same relation holds: a depth and the radius at that place add up to 6,371 km.
The inner core is the ball inside the next boundary, where the liquid outer core meets the solid inner core.
The inner core is therefore a ball about 1,220 km in radius, which is the smallest of the four layers.

lead.text: It is tempting to picture a thin crust floating on a sea of molten rock, but the waves say otherwise. S waves cross the whole mantle, and only a solid can carry them, so the mantle is *solid*. It can still flow, because under great heat and pressure solid rock deforms slowly, over millions of years, in the way a very stiff putty would, and that slow motion is what moves the plates in the next lesson.

The only liquid in the planet is the outer core, a layer of molten iron and nickel that the S-wave shadow reveals. At the centre the pressure is so high that the inner core stays solid even at its very high temperature. Molten rock that reaches volcanoes comes from local melting in the crust and upper mantle, not from a global ocean of magma.

reveal.text: Station D's P waves crossed the core and its S waves were stopped there. That is the evidence that the outer core is liquid, and it is the only liquid layer.
No S-wave shadow means no liquid layer on the way, which is the opposite of what is found on Earth.

lessons.orientation: Earth’s layers and the earthquake waves that revealed them.
lessons.nextAction: Match the three kinds of plate boundary to what happens at each, and calculate how far plates move over geological time.

blocks.text: The deepest hole anyone has drilled, the Kola Superdeep Borehole in north-west Russia, reached 12,262 metres in 1989. That is a remarkable depth for a drill, but the centre of the Earth is 6,371 kilometres from the surface, so the borehole covers only about 0.2 percent of the way down, and the planet below that depth has never been touched.

What we know about it therefore comes from indirect evidence, chiefly from earthquakes, whose waves travel through the whole planet and reach distant seismometers changed by what they have passed through.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to name Earth's layers in order, work out a layer's radius from its depth, and explain how the S-wave shadow showed that the outer core is liquid.
intro.whyItMatters: Almost everything known about the deep Earth comes from waves, so reading them is the first skill of the subject.

recap.keyIdea: Earthquake waves revealed Earth's layers, and because S waves cannot cross a liquid, their shadow shows that the outer core is liquid.

blocks.text: You started from a borehole 12 km deep in a planet of radius 6,371 km, and saw that waves, not drilling, revealed the interior. P waves cross solids and liquids, S waves cross solids only, so the S-wave shadow located a liquid outer core, and the core–mantle boundary at 2,891 km gave a core radius of 3,480 km.
The crust is a thin skin, 7 km thick under oceans and 35 km on continents, and the mantle beneath it is solid rock that flows only over millions of years.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson asks what that slow flow does to the crust above it, and how fast the pieces of crust move.

lessons.title: Plates in motion

lead.text: Wegener had pointed to the fit of the coasts on either side of the Atlantic and to matching rocks and fossils on separate continents, but geologists asked what could push a continent through solid ocean floor, and for decades he had no answer. The answer came from the ocean itself. Surveys from the 1950s found a continuous chain of underwater mountains, the **mid-ocean ridges**, and found that the oceanic crust is youngest at a ridge and grows steadily older with distance from it, with none older than about 200 million years, whereas some continental rock is billions of years old.

The rock at a ridge also keeps a record. Basalt that cools there locks in the direction of Earth's magnetic field at that moment, and because the field has reversed many times, the crust forms stripes of alternating polarity. Ship surveys found that the stripes on one side of a ridge are a mirror image of those on the other, and in 1963 Fred Vine and Drummond Matthews explained why: new crust forms along the ridge and splits down the middle, so that each half carries the same record away in opposite directions. This process is **seafloor spreading**.

afterFigure.text: It follows that the sea floor is not a fixed bed that continents plough across. The sea floor beside a continent is part of the same rigid slab of crust and upper mantle, called a **plate**, and the whole plate moves as one piece.

diagram.alt: Top view of a sea floor either side of a mid-ocean ridge. One view colours the floor by age, youngest at the ridge and oldest furthest away, mirrored on both sides. The other view shows stripes of magnetic polarity that mirror each other across the ridge.

lead.text: Where two plates move **apart** the boundary is **divergent**: magma rises into the gap and cools into new crust, which is what happens along a mid-ocean ridge. Where they move **toward** each other the boundary is **convergent**, and what happens depends on the crust involved. An ocean plate is denser than a continent, so when the two meet the ocean plate sinks beneath, a process called **subduction**, which makes a deep trench in the sea floor, earthquakes along the sinking slab, and volcanoes on the continent above. When two continents meet, neither sinks easily, because both are light, and the crust crumples upward into mountains.

The third kind is the **transform** boundary, where two plates slide past each other along a fault, as the Pacific plate does against the North American plate along the San Andreas Fault. No crust is made or destroyed there, but the plates stick and then slip, and the slip is an earthquake.

afterFigure.text: Earthquakes and volcanoes are therefore not scattered at random. They cluster along plate boundaries, and the largest cluster is the Ring of Fire around the Pacific, where several plates are being subducted.

diagram.alt: Cross-sections and a map view of the three plate boundary types. Divergent: two plates moving apart with magma rising between them. Convergent: an ocean plate sinking under a continent with a trench, earthquakes and a volcano, or two continents crumpling into mountains. Transform: two plates sliding past each other along a fault.

Met earlier in this lesson.]]. The USGS records a magnitude 8.3 earthquake 636 km down in the same subduction zone in 1994.

lead.text: Plate speeds are given in centimetres per year, and geological times in millions of years, so the units need one conversion. A centimetre is 0.01 m, and a million years is 1,000,000 years, so a plate moving 1 cm each year moves 0.01 m × 1,000,000 = 10,000 m in a million years, which is 10 km. That gives a rule worth remembering: **1 cm per year is 10 km per million years**, a million years being written Myr.

To find a distance you therefore multiply the speed in cm per year by 10 to get km per Myr, and then multiply by the number of Myr. A plate at 5 cm per year goes 50 km per Myr, and 200 km in 4 Myr. The same rule works in reverse for a speed: divide a distance in km by a time in Myr to get km per Myr, and then divide by 10 to get cm per year.

steps.headline: A plate moves at 6 cm per year. How far does it move in 30 million years?

workedSteps.text: First turn the speed into km per Myr, using 1 cm per year = 10 km per Myr.
The plate keeps that speed for 30 Myr, and distance is speed multiplied by time.
That is the distance travelled by a plate that moves a few centimetres a year, which shows why a slow rate is not a negligible one.

reveal.text: A rate in centimetres a year turns into kilometres per million years by multiplying by 10, so two plates can be compared only once both speeds are in the same unit.

lead.text: Not every volcano sits on a plate boundary. A **hotspot** is a place where magma rises from deep in the mantle through a plate, and it stays in roughly one place while the plate moves over it. Each time the plate carries a volcano away from the source a new one forms over it, so the surface shows a chain of islands or seamounts, with the youngest at the hotspot and the oldest furthest away. The Hawaiian Islands are a chain of this kind.

The chain is a record of the plate's motion. The distance between two volcanoes, divided by the difference in their ages, gives a speed, and the figure shows the method on a made-up chain of three islands.

afterFigure.text: Here the oldest island is 800 km from the source and 8 Myr old.

diagram.alt: Three stages of a hotspot chain. A fixed hot source sits under a moving plate. After 0 million years there is one island over the source. After 4 million years the first island has moved 400 kilometres away and a new one has formed. After 8 million years there are three islands, the oldest 800 kilometres from the source.
diagram.caption: A made-up chain to show the method. The plate moves and the source stays put, so the islands grow older with distance.

steps.headline: Two islands in a hotspot chain are 480 km apart, and their ages differ by 6 million years. Find the plate speed in cm per year.

workedSteps.text: A speed is a distance divided by a time, so divide the 480 km by the 6 Myr.
That speed is in km per Myr, and 1 cm per year is 10 km per Myr.

reveal.text: The same factor of 10 gives the offset along a fault. The USGS uses this kind of match, a rock formation cut in two, to estimate how fast plates have moved.

recap.keyIdea: Plates meet at divergent, convergent and transform boundaries, and a speed of 1 cm per year is 10 km per million years.

blocks.text: The sea floor is youngest at ridges and carries mirror-image magnetic stripes, which showed that plates, not continents alone, move apart. Where plates move apart, together or past each other, the boundary is divergent, convergent or transform, and each makes its own landforms.
Plate speeds are a few centimetres a year, which is 10 km per million years for every centimetre, so 4 cm per year for 50 million years carries a plate 2,000 km.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson follows the rock itself: how it forms, is buried, melts and returns to the surface.

lessons.title: The rock cycle

reveal.text: The next screens explain how the size of the crystals records the way a rock cooled, and why layers point to a different story.

lead.text: The first of the three rock families is the **igneous** rocks, which form when molten rock cools and solidifies. The crystals grow as the melt cools, and their size depends on how long they have to grow. Magma that cools slowly, deep underground, where the surrounding rock holds heat in, makes large crystals that can be seen by eye, and granite is the usual example. Lava that erupts and cools in hours or days, in contact with air or water, makes crystals too small to see, as in basalt, and lava that cools almost instantly can form volcanic glass with no crystals at all.

This is why the texture of a rock is a kind of history. The same melt that makes basalt at the surface would, if it cooled slowly underground, make a coarse rock called gabbro, so size of crystal tells you about *cooling*, and not only about what the rock is made of.

afterFigure.text: Magma cooling underground is called intrusive, and lava cooling at the surface extrusive.

diagram.alt: Two cross-sections. In one, a body of magma sits underground and cools slowly. In the other, lava erupts from a volcano and cools quickly in contact with air or water.
diagram.caption: Where a melt cools sets how fast it cools. Use the buttons to compare underground with the surface.

reveal.text: Slow cooling underground gives large crystals, and rapid cooling at the surface or under water gives small ones, so the size of the crystals records how fast the rock cooled.

lead.text: The second family begins at the surface. **Weathering** breaks rock into grains and dissolves part of it, and water, wind and ice then carry the material away in **transport**, rounding and sorting it as they go. When the flow slows, the grains settle in **deposition**, forming layers with the oldest at the bottom. Newer layers then bury the older ones, and the weight squeezes the grains together, while water moving through the pores leaves minerals such as silica or calcite that glue the grains into a solid rock, a step called **cementation**. The product is **sedimentary rock**, and its layers record the order in which the grains were deposited.
Layers pile up slowly on average, and the record has long gaps where nothing was deposited or where earlier layers were eroded away.

diagram.alt: Five stages that make a sedimentary rock: weathering breaks rock into grains, transport moves them, deposition lays them in layers, burial compacts them, and cementation glues them into rock.

steps.headline: Mud settles at an average of 0.05 mm per year (an illustrative rate). How long does it take to build 10 m of shale?

workedSteps.text: A rate in millimetres per year needs a thickness in millimetres, so convert 10 m first.
Mud builds up at 0.05 mm per year, and the time is the thickness divided by that rate.
Ten metres of rock thus stands for about 200,000 years of deposition, even though the rate looks tiny. Gaps in the record make the true span longer.

steps.headline: Shale builds up at an average 0.1 mm per year (illustrative). How many years does 50 m take?

workedSteps.text: The rate is in millimetres per year, so the thickness is converted first.
The time is the thickness divided by the rate.

lead.text: The third family forms when existing rock is buried or squeezed, and heated, until its minerals change or regrow while the rock stays solid. The word **metamorphic** means changed in form, and the change is of this kind, not melting. Limestone, made of tiny calcite grains, recrystallises into marble, in which the calcite crystals have grown and interlocked. Shale first becomes slate, which splits along flat surfaces, and with more heat and pressure it becomes schist and then **gneiss**, in which the minerals are separated into coloured bands.

The starting rock may be of any family, which is the point: heat and pressure act on whatever is there. If the temperature rises far enough the rock does melt, and then it is magma, and cooling it makes an igneous rock again.

reveal.text: Heat and pressure acting on solid rock gives a [[metamorphic rock|A rock changed in the solid state by heat and pressure. Met earlier in this lesson.]], whatever the rock was before.

lead.text: The rock cycle is usually drawn as a ring, as though every rock followed the same sequence. The figure shows that this picture is too narrow. Cooling turns melt into igneous rock, weathering and burial turn any exposed rock into sedimentary rock, heat and pressure turn any rock into metamorphic rock, and melting can start from any of them. Igneous rock can become metamorphic without ever being sediment, and sedimentary rock can be buried and melted without becoming metamorphic first.

A rock may also stay in one family for hundreds of millions of years, or pass through the same family twice. The cycle describes what is possible, and the path a particular rock took is read from its crystals, grains and layers.

diagram.alt: A web of arrows between magma, igneous rock, sediment, sedimentary rock and metamorphic rock. Each view highlights one group of routes: cooling, weathering and burial, heat and pressure, or melting. Dashed lines show the other routes.
diagram.caption: The rock cycle as a web, not a ring: any family can reach another by more than one route. Use the buttons to highlight a group of routes.

blocks.text: Granite, the pale speckled stone of many kitchen worktops, is made of crystals you can see: grey quartz, white or pink feldspar and flecks of black mica, each a few millimetres across and locked tightly against its neighbours. Basalt, the dark rock that forms most of the ocean floor, is made of crystals too, but they are too small to see without a lens.

The size of the crystals records something that no one watched happen, which is how quickly the rock cooled from a melt, and the grains and layers of other rocks keep similar records of how they were laid down or changed.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to classify a rock as igneous, sedimentary or metamorphic from how it formed, and read crystal size as a record of cooling.
intro.whyItMatters: A rock's texture records its history, which is how geologists read a landscape.

recap.keyIdea: Igneous, sedimentary and metamorphic rocks form by cooling, deposition and solid-state change, and any rock can pass to any family by more than one route.

blocks.text: You started with crystal size: large crystals mean slow cooling underground, tiny ones mean fast cooling at the surface. Sedimentary rock builds from weathered, carried, deposited and cemented grains, slowly enough that 50 m of shale at 0.1 mm per year stands for half a million years, and metamorphic rock is rock changed in the solid state.
Because any rock can reach any other family by several routes, the rock cycle is a web, not a ring.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson asks how old a rock is, and how radioactive decay gives that age.

lessons.title: Reading deep time

lead.text: Before there was any way to put a date on a rock, geologists could already say which of two rocks was older. In an undisturbed sequence of sedimentary layers the oldest is at the bottom, because each layer has to be laid down on top of one that already exists, and a fault or an igneous intrusion that cuts across layers must be younger than the layers it cuts. These rules give a *relative* age, a sequence of events with no numbers attached.

Sedimentary sequences, ice cores and radioactive isotopes taken together show that Earth's record runs to millions and billions of years, and an **absolute age**, a date in years, needs a clock that runs at a known rate. Radioactive decay is such a clock.

reveal.text: The next screen explains the rule, and why the sample is not simply gone after twice the half-life.

lead.text: A single radioactive atom decays at an unpredictable moment, but a large number of identical atoms decay in a perfectly regular pattern. The **half-life** of an isotope is the time in which half of them decay, and it is a fixed property of the isotope: 5,730 years for carbon-14, and 4.468 billion years for uranium-238. After one half-life half of the atoms remain, after two a quarter, after three an eighth, and in general after *n* half-lives a fraction (1/2)ⁿ is left.

afterFigure.text: The curve in the figure has the same shape for every isotope, and only the time scale changes. This is what makes dating possible: if you can measure what fraction of the original isotope is left, you can read off how many half-lives have passed, and multiply by the half-life to get the age.

A decaying atom becomes an atom of another element, so carbon-14 becomes nitrogen-14, and uranium-238, through a chain of steps, ends as lead-206. The decaying isotope is called the **parent** and the product the **daughter**, and as the parent dwindles the daughter builds up, so in a sample that began with no daughter atoms every daughter atom stands for one parent atom that has decayed.

steps.headline: A bone has 1/8 of its original carbon-14. The half-life of carbon-14 is 5,730 years. How old is the bone?

workedSteps.text: Find how many halvings take the fraction from 1 to 1/8: 1/2, then 1/4, then 1/8.
Each half-life lasts 5,730 years, and the age is the number of half-lives times that.
The bone died about 17,000 years ago, and the same steps work for any fraction that is a power of 1/2.

steps.headline: Date a rock with one part parent isotope to three parts daughter, with a half-life of 700 million years.

workedSteps.text: Every decayed parent atom became a daughter atom, so a rock with 1 part parent to 3 parts daughter has 1 part parent out of 4 in all.
The half-life is 700 million years.

lead.text: The fraction left must be large enough to measure and small enough to differ from the start, so each isotope suits a limited range of ages. Carbon-14 is made in the atmosphere and taken up by living things, and it stops being replaced when they die. Its half-life is short, and after about 50,000 years too little remains to measure, so radiocarbon dating is used for bone, wood and charcoal from the recent past. It cannot date a rock that is millions of years old.

Rocks are dated with isotopes of long half-life. Uranium-238 decays to lead-206 with a half-life of 4.468 billion years, and a mineral that formed with uranium and no lead holds a record of the time since it crystallised, in the ratio of lead to uranium.

reveal.text: After 50,000 years carbon-14 has almost gone, but uranium-238 has hardly started its first half-life.
A rock cannot be older than the planet, so a reading that gives more than 4.54 billion years has to be a misreading. Sample B's three half-lives of uranium-238 come to 13.5 billion years.

lead.text: In the 1950s Clair Patterson measured the lead isotopes in meteorites, which formed with the rest of the Solar System, and reported in 1956 an age of about 4.55 billion years. Later work on meteorites and on the oldest minerals of Earth gives the age of the planet as about 4.54 billion years, and the oldest minerals found on Earth, zircon grains from Western Australia, are about 4.4 billion years old.

Suppose the whole 4,540 million years is scaled to 24 hours, so that Earth forms at midnight and today is the following midnight. An event *t* million years ago then falls t ÷ 4,540 of a day before the end, and since a day is 1,440 minutes the time before midnight in minutes is t ÷ 4,540 × 1,440.

afterFigure.text: On that clock the oldest minerals appear at 00:44, life at around 05:30, the rise of oxygen at 11:19 and animals at 21:09. All of what follows, including the dinosaurs and modern humans, is crowded into the last few hours.

diagram.alt: Earth history scaled to one 24-hour day. The first view marks the oldest minerals at 00:44, first life at 05:30, the rise of oxygen at 11:19 and animals at 21:09. The second view shows the last 30 minutes, with the dinosaur extinction at 23:39 and modern humans in the last few seconds.
diagram.caption: Earth’s 4,540 million years compressed into 24 hours. Use the buttons to see the whole day and then its last half hour.

reveal.text: The first dinosaurs appear at about 22:47, and their extinction, at 23:39 in the figure, leaves only 21 minutes of the day for all the time since.
Earth forms at midnight and today is the next midnight, so each hour on the clock stands for 4,540 ÷ 24, about 189 million years.

lessons.orientation: Dating samples by half-life, and the age of Earth.
lessons.nextAction: Say what the atmosphere is made of and how pressure falls with height.

blocks.text: A single carbon-14 atom in a bone has no schedule: it may decay in the next second or in the next hundred thousand years. A large number of such atoms, however, decay with perfect regularity, since half of them are gone after 5,730 years whatever the size of the sample. Carbon-14 is one **isotope** of carbon, a form of the element whose atoms carry two more neutrons than those of ordinary carbon-12, and the extra neutrons leave it unstable.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to date a sample from the fraction of an isotope left, and scale Earth's age onto a 24-hour clock.
intro.whyItMatters: Radioactive decay is the one dependable clock in deep time, and it puts every rock and fossil in the same calendar.

recap.keyIdea: After n half-lives a fraction (1/2)ⁿ of an isotope remains, so the fraction left gives an age, and Earth is about 4.54 billion years old.

blocks.text: A half-life is the time for half of the atoms to decay, so a sample with 1/8 of its carbon-14 is three half-lives, or 17,190 years, old. Carbon-14 reaches only about 50,000 years back, so rocks are dated with long-lived isotopes such as uranium-238, and a ratio of one part parent to three of daughter means a fraction of 1/4 and two half-lives.
On a clock where Earth's 4,540 million years is one day, the first dinosaurs arrive 73 minutes before midnight and modern humans in the last six seconds.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson turns from the solid Earth to the air above it, and from time to pressure and height.

lessons.title: Layers of air

reveal.text: The thin air is the real difficulty at the summit, and a later screen separates the mix from the pressure.

lead.text: Dry air is 78.08 percent nitrogen, 20.95 percent oxygen and 0.93 percent argon by volume, with carbon dioxide at about 0.04 percent and traces of other gases, and these proportions hold from the ground to well above the highest mountains because the winds keep the air mixed. Water vapour is the variable part, amounting to up to a few percent near the surface in warm, humid air and very little in cold, dry air.

**Pressure** is the force that a gas exerts on a surface, per unit of area, and in the atmosphere it is the weight of the column of air above that surface. At sea level the air presses on each square metre with a force of about 101,300 newtons, which is why the standard sea-level pressure is written as 101.3 kPa (kilopascals), or 1,013 hPa. Because a column from higher up has less air above it, pressure falls with height.

Near the surface the fall in pressure follows a simple rule: it halves for every 5.5 km of height. At 5.5 km the pressure is half of 101.3 kPa, 50.65 kPa, at 11 km it is half of that again, 25.3 kPa, and at 16.5 km it is 12.7 kPa. Half of the mass of the atmosphere therefore lies below 5.5 km, which is lower than the summits of the highest mountains.

The rule is an approximation, and the real pressure at 11 km, in a standard atmosphere, is a little lower, about 22.6 kPa. It is accurate enough to give the size of an effect, and for any height the number of halvings is the height divided by 5.5 km.

afterFigure.text: For Everest the number of halvings is 8.85 ÷ 5.5, about 1.6, which gives about 33 kPa, a third of the sea-level value. Oxygen is still 21 percent of the air, but its own pressure is 21 percent of 33 kPa, about 7 kPa, and it is the pressure, not the percentage, that decides how much oxygen a breath delivers.

steps.headline: On a high-pressure day sea-level pressure is 104.0 kPa, and pressure halves every 5.5 km. Find the pressure at 11 km, where airliners cruise.

workedSteps.text: Count the halvings: the height divided by 5.5 km.
Each halving divides the pressure by 2, so two halvings divide it by 4.
The outside air pressure at cruising height is thus about a quarter of sea level.

steps.headline: On a day of low pressure, sea-level pressure is 99.2 kPa. Find the pressure at 16.5 km, where the same rule applies.

workedSteps.text: The number of halvings is the height divided by 5.5 km.
Each halving cuts the pressure to half of what it was.

reveal.text: The rule is a good guide near the ground. At 11 km, where airliners cruise, it is about a tenth too high, and the error keeps growing with height.

lead.text: Temperature does not simply fall with height. In the **troposphere**, the lowest layer, it falls with height, by about 6.5 °C for each kilometre on average, because the air is warmed from below by the ground, which absorbs sunlight. The top of the troposphere is about 12 km up on average, higher in the tropics and lower near the poles. Above it lies the **stratosphere**, where temperature *rises* with height, because the ozone there absorbs ultraviolet light from the Sun and warms the air around it. At about 50 km the temperature turns again, and in the **mesosphere** it falls to its lowest in the atmosphere, near 85 km, before rising once more in the **thermosphere**, where the air is extremely thin and absorbs the most energetic solar radiation.

afterFigure.text: The figure is schematic, and the values vary with place and season, but the shape, a zigzag with three turns, is the same everywhere.

Temperature falls through the troposphere to about 12 kilometres, rises through the stratosphere to about 50 kilometres, falls through the mesosphere to about 85 kilometres and rises again in the thermosphere. A second view labels the cause of the rise in the stratosphere.

reveal.text: The temperature stops falling at about 11 km, the top of the troposphere, and rises again from about 25 km. That rise is the sign of the stratosphere, heated from above by ozone and not from the ground.

lead.text: The troposphere holds about three quarters of the mass of the atmosphere, together with almost all of its water vapour, and because it is warmed from below its air rises and sinks, which is the engine of the clouds, winds and storms of later lessons. The stratosphere above is stable, since warm air lies over cold, so air there does not rise and fall in the same way, and this is why airliners cruise near the top of the troposphere, in smooth air above most of the weather.

Nor is there a sharp edge to the atmosphere. The pressure keeps falling by half at every step, so the air thins gradually, and the 100 km altitude that is often called the edge of space, the Karman line, is a convention rather than a boundary in the air itself.

reveal.text: Pressure is the weight of the air above, so a quarter of the sea-level pressure means a quarter of the atmosphere's mass lies above 11 km, which is why the air inside an airliner has to be pressurised.

lessons.orientation: What the air is made of, how pressure falls with height, and the four layers of the atmosphere.
lessons.nextAction: Compute the sunlight Earth absorbs, and compare it with the heat that Earth would radiate with no greenhouse gases.

blocks.text: At sea level the air presses on every square metre with a force of about 101,300 newtons, roughly the weight of ten tonnes, because that is the weight of the column of air standing above the square metre and reaching to the top of the atmosphere. We feel nothing of it, since the air inside our bodies pushes back with the same pressure, but the weight is real, and the column above a mountain summit is shorter.
On the summit of Mount Everest only about a third of that air lies overhead, which gives a pressure near 33 kPa, so each breath there takes in far less oxygen than the same breath at sea level.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to estimate air pressure at any height with the halving rule and name the four layers in order.
intro.whyItMatters: Weather, flight and climbing all depend on how pressure and temperature change with height.

recap.keyIdea: Pressure is the weight of the air above and halves every 5.5 km, and temperature turns three times with height to give four layers.

blocks.text: The air is 78.08 percent nitrogen and 20.95 percent oxygen at every height, so what changes on a mountain is the pressure, which halves every 5.5 km: 25.3 kPa at 11 km, and 12.7 kPa at 16.5 km. The oxygen share stays at 21 percent, but its pressure falls with the total.
Temperature falls in the troposphere, rises in the stratosphere because ozone absorbs ultraviolet, falls in the mesosphere and rises in the thermosphere, and nearly all weather is in the troposphere.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson asks how much sunlight the surface and atmosphere absorb, and how a layer of gas changes the balance.

lessons.title: The energy balance

reveal.text: The next screen compares the disc with the sphere, and the screens after it use the result to find what the planet actually absorbs.

lead.text: The power of sunlight at Earth's distance, measured on a surface held square to the rays, is about 1,361 watts per square metre. That figure cannot be used for the whole planet, because a planet intercepts sunlight over a *disc*, the circle that the Sun sees, which has an area of πr², while the energy is shared by the whole *sphere*, which has an area of 4πr². The sphere has four times the area of the disc, so the average power on each square metre of the planet's surface is 1,361 ÷ 4, which is about 340 W/m².

diagram.alt: Two views of sunlight reaching a planet. In the first, parallel rays strike a planet and the part they can reach is a flat disc of area pi r squared. In the second, the same energy is spread over the whole sphere, whose area is four pi r squared, four times as large.
diagram.caption: The Sun lights a disc but the energy is shared by a sphere. Use the buttons to compare the two areas.

lead.text: Not all the sunlight is absorbed. Clouds, ice, bright land and the air reflect part of it straight back to space, and the fraction reflected is called the **albedo**. Earth's albedo is about 0.30, so about 30 percent is reflected and 70 percent, a fraction 1 − 0.30, is absorbed. Fresh snow has a high albedo and the open ocean a low one, and the planet's value is the average over all of them.
The absorbed power per square metre of the planet's surface is therefore 1,361 × (1 − albedo) ÷ 4.

steps.headline: Find the average power that Earth absorbs per square metre, with an albedo of 0.30.

workedSteps.text: Take the share absorbed, one minus the albedo.
The absorbed power is the intercepted power times that share, divided by 4 because the planet is a sphere.
About 238 W/m² of the 340 arriving is absorbed, and about 102 is reflected.

steps.headline: A planet at the same distance has an albedo of 0.5. Find the power it absorbs per square metre.

workedSteps.text: The share absorbed is one minus the albedo.
The planet is a sphere again, so the intercepted power is divided by 4.

lead.text: For the temperature to stay steady, the planet must send out as much energy as it absorbs. A surface at temperature T, in kelvin, emits energy per square metre equal to σT⁴, where σ = 5.67 × 10⁻⁸ W/m²/K⁴ is the **Stefan–Boltzmann constant**, and the energy comes out as infrared radiation. Setting σT⁴ equal to the absorbed 238 W/m² and solving for T gives T = (238 ÷ 5.67 × 10⁻⁸)^(1/4), which is about 255 K, or about −18 °C.
The fourth power matters: doubling the temperature raises the emission sixteen times. It also means that an *increase* in absorbed power raises the balancing temperature only slowly.

The observed global mean surface temperature is about 288 K, or 15 °C, and a bare Earth would be at 255 K, so the surface is about 33 K warmer than the simple calculation says. The difference is the **greenhouse effect**, and it is a natural feature of the planet, not a fault of pollution. Water vapour, carbon dioxide, methane and other **greenhouse gases** let the sunlight through but absorb the infrared that the surface emits, and they then re-emit it in all directions, including downward.

The popular picture of a glass lid that traps heat is misleading, since nothing is held in. The surface at 288 K emits σT⁴, about 390 W/m², yet only 238 W/m² leaves at the top of the atmosphere. The 152 W/m² difference is infrared that gases absorb and send back, partly toward the surface, which changes the *way* energy leaves and so sets a warmer surface for the same balance.

afterFigure.text: Adding more greenhouse gases strengthens an effect that already exists.

diagram.alt: Energy arrows for a bare Earth and for the real Earth. Both receive 340 watts per square metre of sunlight, reflect 102 and absorb 238, and both send 238 out to space. On the real Earth the surface emits 390 because gases in the air absorb some of that infrared and send part of it back down.

reveal.text: Sunlight passes through the gases mostly as visible light, and the surface gives the energy back as infrared, which the gases absorb. Part of what they send out goes back down, so less of the surface's infrared reaches space.
Venus absorbs less sunlight per square metre than Earth, because it reflects 77 percent of it, and yet its surface is far hotter. The extra heat comes from its atmosphere.

lessons.orientation: The energy that Earth absorbs from the Sun, the temperature it would have without an atmosphere, and the greenhouse effect.
lessons.nextAction: Explain wind, fronts and cloud from pressure, rotation and rising air.

blocks.text: Take an Earth with no atmosphere, give it the Sun's output and Earth's reflectivity, and a short calculation gives its average surface temperature as about 255 kelvin, or −18 °C, far below freezing. The measured average of the real surface is about 288 kelvin, which is 15 °C, so something in the air makes it 33 kelvin warmer than the calculation says.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to calculate the sunlight Earth absorbs, find the temperature that balances it, and say why the real surface is 33 K warmer.
intro.whyItMatters: The energy balance is the starting point for every question about climate.

recap.keyIdea: The planet absorbs 1,361 × (1 − albedo) ÷ 4 W/m² and balances it at 255 K, and greenhouse gases make the surface 33 K warmer.

blocks.text: Sunlight of 1,361 W/m² is spread over a sphere with four times the disc's area, and with an albedo of 0.30 the planet absorbs about 238 W/m². The Stefan–Boltzmann law turns that balance into a temperature of 255 K, against the observed 288 K.
The difference of 33 K is the natural greenhouse effect: gases absorb outgoing infrared and radiate part of it back downward.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson moves from the average to the weather, and from energy to the winds that carry it.

lessons.title: Why the weather moves

lead.text: Sunlight warms the land more quickly than the sea. By day the air over a coast is warmed from below and rises, which lowers the pressure at the surface over the land, and the cooler air over the sea, at higher pressure, flows in to replace it as a **sea breeze**. Aloft the air flows back the other way, so the movement forms a closed loop. By night the land cools faster, and the loop reverses.
The rule behind it is general. **Wind** is air moving in response to a pressure difference, and the steeper the change in pressure across a distance, the stronger the wind.

diagram.alt: Cross-sections of a coast. By day the land is warmer, so air rises over land and a sea breeze blows in at the surface toward the lower pressure, with a return flow aloft. By night the land is cooler, so the flow reverses into a land breeze.
diagram.caption: Uneven heating makes a pressure difference, and air moves from high pressure to low. Use the buttons to compare day and night.

reveal.text: The next screen names this turning effect and shows the spiral on a map.

lead.text: Because Earth rotates, air that moves over long distances is deflected, an effect called the **Coriolis effect**: to the right of its motion in the Northern Hemisphere and to the left in the Southern. Air that starts to flow toward a low is therefore turned as it goes, and the balance of the pressure difference with the deflection leaves it moving nearly along the lines of equal pressure aloft, rather than across them. The result is a spiral inward at the surface, counterclockwise around a low in the Northern Hemisphere and clockwise in the Southern, with the opposite pattern around a high.

afterFigure.text: Wind therefore does not blow straight from high pressure to low. It is turned by the rotation, and the circulations around highs and lows are what weather maps show.

diagram.alt: Map views of air flowing toward a low-pressure centre. Without rotation the arrows go straight in. In the Northern Hemisphere the rotation of Earth deflects the flow to the right, so the arrows spiral in counterclockwise. In the Southern Hemisphere the deflection is to the left, so they spiral in clockwise.
diagram.caption: Looking down on a low-pressure centre, with dashed lines of equal pressure. Use the buttons to compare no rotation with each hemisphere.

lead.text: The tropics receive more sunlight than the poles, so air rises there, flows poleward aloft, and sinks near 30 degrees latitude, a loop called the Hadley cell. At the surface, air flowing back toward the equator is deflected westward, which makes the **trade winds**, blowing from the east. Between about 30 and 60 degrees, the surface winds blow from the west, the **westerlies**, and near the poles cold air flows outward and is deflected into the **polar easterlies**. Between the belts the air meets or splits, and these regions are where much of the weather in the middle latitudes is made.

reveal.text: In the south, every Northern Hemisphere pattern is mirrored, so a high turns counterclockwise there.

lead.text: Warm air rises, but it does not keep warming as it rises. Pressure falls with height, as in the lesson on layers of air, so a parcel of rising air expands, and the expansion costs it energy, so it *cools*, by about 9.8 °C for each kilometre while it stays unsaturated. The **dew point** is the temperature at which the air is saturated and water vapour begins to condense, and it falls too, but more slowly, by about 1.8 °C per kilometre. The two lines approach each other at about 8 °C per kilometre, and where they meet the vapour condenses into a **cloud**.

The height where this happens is the cloud base, and since the lines close at 8 °C per kilometre it is about 125 metres for each degree of the gap between the temperature and the dew point at the surface.

afterFigure.text: With a 10-degree gap the lines meet at 1.25 km, and with a 4-degree gap at 0.5 km. Humid air makes low clouds, and dry air makes clouds that form high or not at all.

diagram.alt: Temperature and dew point of a rising parcel of air against height. The air temperature falls by 9.8 degrees per kilometre and the dew point by about 1.8 degrees per kilometre, so the two lines meet at the cloud base. A gap of 10 degrees at the ground gives a cloud base at 1,250 metres. A gap of 4 degrees gives 500 metres.

steps.headline: At the surface the air is at 30 °C and its dew point is 18 °C. Find the cloud base.

workedSteps.text: Find the gap between temperature and dew point.
The cloud base is 125 metres for each degree of the gap.
The cloud base is 1.5 km up, a little above the 1.25 km that the figure draws for a 10-degree gap.

steps.headline: The air is at 24 °C and the dew point is 10 °C. Find the cloud base.

workedSteps.text: The gap between the temperature and the dew point comes first.
Each degree of that gap raises the cloud base by 125 m.

reveal.text: The gap between the temperature and the dew point closes as the evening air cools, so the cloud base comes down until, at midnight, it reaches the ground.

lead.text: A **front** is the boundary between two air masses of different temperature. At a cold front, dense cold air pushes under warmer air and lifts it steeply, which can make tall clouds and heavy showers, and at a warm front warm air slides up over the cold air along a gentle slope and makes broad layers of cloud. In both cases the warm air is lifted, cools, and reaches its dew point.

Weather and climate are not the same. **Weather** is the state of the atmosphere at a place and time: its temperature, wind, cloud and rain. **Climate** is the long-term pattern of weather, usually averaged over 30 years, and a cold week does not change it.

reveal.text: A wide gap between the temperature and the dew point means dry air, which has to rise a long way before its vapour condenses, and a narrow gap means a low cloud base.

lessons.orientation: Wind as a response to pressure differences, how rotation shapes it, and how rising air forms cloud.
lessons.nextAction: Explain how density drives the deep ocean circulation, and calculate sea-level change from added water.

blocks.text: On a hot afternoon at the coast the wind comes in from the sea, and at night it turns round and blows from the land. Nothing has pushed the air in either direction, but the land has warmed or cooled faster than the water, so the pressure over it has fallen or risen, and air moves from the region of higher pressure to the lower. The same cause, on a planet-wide scale and with the Earth's rotation added, produces trade winds and storms.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to say how air circulates around a low or high, and find the height of cloud base from temperature and dew point.
intro.whyItMatters: The same few rules explain a sea breeze, a storm and the height of a cloud.

recap.keyIdea: Wind blows from high toward low pressure and is deflected by Earth's rotation, and rising air cools until its dew point sets the cloud base.

blocks.text: Uneven heating makes pressure differences, and air flows from higher pressure toward lower while the Coriolis effect turns it right in the north and left in the south, so lows circulate counterclockwise in the north and clockwise in the south. Rising air cools by 9.8 °C per kilometre, and the cloud base lies 125 metres up for each degree between the temperature and the dew point, which is 1,500 m for air at 30 °C with a dew point of 18 °C.
Weather is the state of the air now and climate is its pattern over about 30 years.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson turns to the ocean, where differences in density drive a slow circulation.

lessons.title: The ocean system

reveal.text: The next screen shows what sets the density of seawater, and the one after it how sinking water drives the deep circulation of the ocean.

lead.text: The ocean covers about 71 percent of Earth's surface, and its mean depth is about 3,700 m. Its water holds about 35 grams of dissolved salt in each kilogram, a measure called **salinity**, and the density of seawater depends on two things: temperature and salinity. Cooling seawater makes it denser, because the water contracts, and adding salt makes it denser, because the salt adds mass to a very slightly larger volume. Water that is both cold and salty is therefore the densest, and warm fresh water the least dense.
Density decides where water goes: dense water sinks beneath lighter water, and lighter water floats above it.

Two systems move the ocean's water. At the surface the winds push on the water, and the Coriolis effect turns it, so the water circulates in large loops called **gyres**, one in each of the main ocean basins. The Gulf Stream, which carries warm water north along the east coast of North America and across the Atlantic, is part of such a gyre.

Below the surface a different driver works. In the North Atlantic and near Antarctica, water at the surface cools and also becomes saltier as sea ice forms and leaves its salt behind, so it becomes dense enough to sink. It spreads along the bottom of the ocean and, many centuries later, rises again elsewhere. This slow density-driven flow, which links the surface and the deep, is the **overturning circulation**.

afterFigure.text: Currents in the deep ocean are driven by density, and they carry heat and dissolved gases between the surface and the deep.

reveal.text: Differences in density, set by temperature and salinity, are what make water sink at high latitudes.

lead.text: Water has a large heat capacity and there is a great deal of it, so the ocean holds most of the heat in the climate system. According to the IPCC's Sixth Assessment Report, ocean warming accounts for about 91 percent of the energy gained by the climate system between 1971 and 2018. Warmer water also expands, which raises sea level without any water being added, and this **thermal expansion** explained about half of the rise between 1971 and 2018, with glaciers, the ice sheets and land water storage making up the rest.

Ice matters in two ways. Floating ice, such as sea ice or an ice shelf, already displaces its own weight of water, so its melting leaves the level unchanged. Ice on land, in glaciers and the ice sheets of Greenland and Antarctica, is not in the water, so when it melts it adds new water to the ocean. A volume of land ice melts to about 0.92 of its volume of water.

reveal.text: The same reasoning applies to a floating ice shelf, and it does not apply to ice resting on land.

lead.text: The size of the rise can be found by spreading the added water over the whole ocean as a layer. The ocean's area is about 361 million km², and a layer of volume V over an area A has a depth of V ÷ A. If 18,050 km³ of water is added, the depth is 18,050 ÷ 361,000,000 km, which is 0.00005 km, or 5 cm, and so 1 mm of sea level needs 361 km³. The method gives an estimate, since the ocean's area changes slightly as the level rises and the water does not spread perfectly evenly, but it is accurate enough to show the size of an effect.

steps.headline: Spread 3,610 km³ of added water over an ocean of area 361 million km². Find the rise in sea level, in millimetres.

workedSteps.text: The depth of the layer is the volume divided by the area.
The depth is in kilometres, and there are 1,000,000 mm in a kilometre.
So 361 km³ of water raises the ocean by 1 mm, a number worth remembering.

steps.headline: Do the same with 7,220 km³ of meltwater.

workedSteps.text: The depth of the added layer is the volume divided by the ocean's area of 361 million km².
A kilometre is 1,000,000 mm.

reveal.text: Each rate multiplied by its years gives 91, 66.5 and 44.4 mm, which add to about 0.20 m. More than half of that rise came after 1971.
Add the two losses, count each billion tonnes as 1 km³ of water, and divide by the 361 km³ that make a millimetre.

lessons.orientation: How seawater density drives the deep ocean circulation, and how added water and expansion raise sea level.
lessons.nextAction: Track carbon between reservoirs and convert between gigatonnes of carbon, of carbon dioxide and parts per million.

blocks.text: The Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change reports in its Sixth Assessment Report that global mean sea level rose 0.20 metres between 1901 and 2018, and that the rate of rise reached 3.7 millimetres a year in 2006 to 2018. The ocean covers 361 million square kilometres, so a rise of 3.7 millimetres a year corresponds to about 1,300 cubic kilometres of water, or its equivalent in expansion, added every year.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to say which water sinks and why, and calculate the rise in sea level from a volume of added water.
intro.whyItMatters: The ocean stores most of the extra heat, and its level is the clearest measure of how much has been added.

recap.keyIdea: Cold salty water sinks and drives the deep circulation, and sea-level rise equals added volume divided by ocean area, 361 km³ per millimetre.

blocks.text: Seawater is densest when it is cold and salty, so water sinks in the North Atlantic and near Antarctica and returns slowly, while wind drives only the surface gyres. Ocean warming accounts for about 91 percent of the energy gained by the climate system from 1971 to 2018, and thermal expansion explained about half of the sea-level rise in that period.
Floating ice does not raise the level when it melts, but land ice does, and since 361 km³ of water raises the ocean by 1 mm, 7,220 km³ raises it by 20 mm.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson follows carbon, the element at the centre of the climate story, between the air, the ocean, the land and the rocks.

lessons.title: How carbon moves

lead.text: Carbon moves between a handful of reservoirs. The atmosphere holds about 900 GtC (gigatonnes of carbon, billions of tonnes) at the carbon dioxide level of 2023, the land holds roughly 450 to 650 GtC in plants and 1,500 to 2,400 GtC in soils, and the ocean holds about 38,000 GtC, mostly as dissolved carbon, so the ocean is by far the largest of the reservoirs that exchange carbon with the air in less than a century. Rocks and sediments hold tens of millions of GtC, far more than all the rest together.

The flows have different speeds. In the **fast cycle**, plants take up about 120 GtC a year by photosynthesis and return nearly as much by respiration and decay, and the ocean surface exchanges carbon dioxide with the air in a similar balance, over years to decades. In the **slow cycle**, weathering and burial remove carbon from the air into rocks and volcanoes return it, over thousands to millions of years. Human emissions, of about 10 GtC a year from fossil fuels, are a new flow into the fast cycle.

afterFigure.text: The natural flows are large, but they roughly cancel from year to year, which is why carbon dioxide stayed near 280 ppm for thousands of years before industry. Human emissions are small beside either flow, and they are the part that does not cancel.

diagram.alt: Boxes for the carbon reservoirs. The fast cycle links the atmosphere, about 900 GtC, with land plants and soils and with the ocean, about 38,000 GtC, with plant exchange near 120 GtC a year and fossil fuel emissions of 10.2 GtC in 2024. The slow cycle links the atmosphere with rocks and sediments through weathering, burial and volcanoes over thousands to millions of years.

reveal.text: The next screen explains the units: carbon atoms have a mass of 12 and oxygen atoms 16, and carbon dioxide has one carbon and two oxygens.

lead.text: Carbon emissions are quoted in two ways, and mixing them up is the commonest error. A carbon dioxide molecule has one carbon atom, of mass 12, and two oxygen atoms, of mass 16 each, so the molecule has a mass of 44, and carbon is 12/44 of the mass of the CO₂. To convert a mass of carbon to a mass of carbon dioxide you multiply by 44/12, about 3.67, and to go back you multiply by 12/44. Thus 3 GtC is 3 × 44/12 = 11 GtCO₂.

A third unit is the concentration in the air, in **parts per million**, or ppm, the number of CO₂ molecules in every million molecules of air. About 2.13 GtC in the atmosphere corresponds to 1 ppm, so a mass of carbon added to the air divides by 2.13 to give a rise in ppm. The Global Carbon Project reports emissions in GtCO₂, so its figures have to be converted before they can be set beside a mass of carbon in the air.

steps.headline: Convert 10 GtC of carbon emissions to a mass of carbon dioxide.

workedSteps.text: A mass of carbon is multiplied by 44/12 to give the mass of carbon dioxide.
That factor applies to the whole 10 GtC.
The same 10 GtC can be written as 36.7 GtCO₂, and the two numbers describe the same carbon.

steps.headline: The Global Carbon Project reported fossil CO₂ emissions of 37.4 GtCO₂ in 2024. Convert this to GtC.

workedSteps.text: Carbon is 12 of the 44 mass units in carbon dioxide.
The reported figure counts whole molecules of carbon dioxide, and carbon is only part of each.

reveal.text: The two figures describe the same emission, 11.1 GtC and 40.6 GtCO₂, so they have to be in one unit before either is compared with the 5.9 GtC in the air.

lead.text: Not all of the carbon emitted stays in the atmosphere. Plants and soils take up part of it and the ocean takes up part, so only a fraction, the **airborne fraction**, builds up in the air. The Global Carbon Project finds that this is close to half in recent decades, and this lesson uses a round 45 percent. Using it, emissions of 6 GtC in a year leave 2.7 GtC in the air, and dividing by 2.13 GtC per ppm gives a rise of 1.3 ppm.

The air is *not* receiving all the carbon, and yet the concentration keeps rising, because the natural flows nearly balance each other and the extra from humans sits on top of them, so what is left over after the land and ocean have taken their share still accumulates.

steps.headline: Emissions are 10 GtC in a year, 45 percent stays in the air, and 2.13 GtC raises CO₂ by 1 ppm. Find the rise in CO₂ over the year.

workedSteps.text: The carbon that stays in the air is the airborne fraction of the emissions.
Each 2.13 GtC in the air raises the concentration by 1 ppm.
A rise of about 2.1 ppm in a year is the size of change that the Mauna Loa record shows.

reveal.text: About 53 percent of the emissions stayed in the air in 2023, a little above the round 45 percent used here. The share changes from year to year.

lead.text: Charles David Keeling began measuring carbon dioxide at Mauna Loa, in Hawaii, in March 1958, far from local sources, and the record has run ever since. The NOAA Global Monitoring Laboratory gives the annual mean as 315.98 ppm in 1959, 421.08 ppm in 2023 and 424.61 ppm in 2024. The curve rises every year, and the rise is the airborne fraction of emissions.

Each year also has a wiggle of several ppm. In the northern summer the plants take up carbon dioxide and the concentration falls to a low in autumn, and in the winter respiration and decay return it, so the peak comes in May.

afterFigure.text: Before industry the level was about 280 ppm; the Global Carbon Project takes 278 ppm for 1750. The 2023 mean is therefore more than 50 percent above it.

lessons.orientation: Where carbon is stored, how it moves, and the units used to count it.
lessons.nextAction: Relate forcing to warming and weigh the evidence that the recent change is human-driven.

blocks.text: The NOAA Global Monitoring Laboratory reports that the annual mean concentration of carbon dioxide at Mauna Loa was 315.98 parts per million in 1959, the first full year of measurement, and 421.08 in 2023, a gain of about 105 ppm in 64 years.

A concentration can be turned into a mass of carbon, and a mass of carbon into a mass of carbon dioxide, and since climate figures are quoted in all three units, a figure read in the wrong one can be far out.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to convert between GtC, GtCO₂ and ppm, and work out how much of a year's emissions raises the CO₂ level.
intro.whyItMatters: Every climate figure is quoted in one of these units, and a figure read in the wrong one gives a badly wrong answer.

recap.keyIdea: Carbon is 12/44 of the mass of CO₂, 2.13 GtC in the air is 1 ppm, and about 45 percent of emissions stays airborne.

blocks.text: Carbon moves between the atmosphere, land, ocean and rocks, quickly in the fast cycle and slowly in the slow cycle, and human emissions of 10.2 GtC in 2024 add to a fast cycle whose natural flows roughly cancel. A mass of carbon is multiplied by 44/12 to give carbon dioxide, so 10 GtC is 36.7 GtCO₂.
If 45 percent of 10 GtC stays in the air, that is 4.5 GtC, which at 2.13 GtC per ppm raises CO₂ by 2.1 ppm in a year, and the Mauna Loa record shows that rise beneath a seasonal wiggle.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson asks how a change in carbon dioxide becomes a change in temperature, and what the evidence says about its cause.

lessons.title: What has changed and why

lead.text: Air bubbles trapped in Antarctic ice preserve samples of the atmosphere of the past 800,000 years. In that record the concentration of carbon dioxide stays between about 180 ppm in the cold ice ages and about 280 ppm in the warm periods between them, and temperature and CO₂ rose and fell together, over cycles of roughly 100,000 years that were set off by slow changes in Earth's orbit.

Climate has therefore changed naturally before, and the record of those changes is what lets us measure the causes. Orbital changes act over tens of thousands of years, whereas the rise from 280 to above 410 ppm took under 300 years, and it is this speed, and not the fact of change, that needs explaining.

reveal.text: The next screen gives the rule in a formula, and shows what it implies for a doubling.

lead.text: A **radiative forcing** is a change in the energy balance of the planet, in W/m², caused by something outside the climate system's ordinary response, such as more greenhouse gas, volcanic dust or a change in the Sun. A positive forcing means that the planet absorbs more energy than it sends back. For carbon dioxide a standard formula, from Myhre and colleagues in 1998, gives the forcing relative to a reference concentration C₀ as 5.35 × ln(C ÷ C₀), where ln is the natural logarithm.

Taking C₀ = 280 ppm, a rise to 700 ppm, two and a half times as much, gives 5.35 × ln 2.5 = 4.9 W/m². Because the logarithm turns each doubling into the same step, *every* doubling adds the same forcing, so going from 560 to 1,120 ppm adds as much as going from 280 to 560.

afterFigure.text: The curve rises quickly at first and then flattens, which is what a logarithm does, and the flattening has a physical cause. Carbon dioxide absorbs infrared strongly in a few **absorption bands**, narrow ranges of wavelength, and at the centres of those bands the air already absorbs almost all the infrared that the surface sends up, so extra CO₂ acts mainly at the edges of the bands, where absorption is weaker, and each added ppm counts for less than the one before.

diagram.alt: Two views of the forcing from carbon dioxide relative to 280 ppm. A curve that rises steeply and then flattens shows 4.9 W per square metre at 700 ppm. Two equal bars show that each doubling, 280 to 560 and 560 to 1,120, adds the same forcing.
diagram.caption: Forcing grows with the logarithm of concentration. Use the buttons to see the curve and the equal doublings.

steps.headline: Find the forcing for a doubling of CO₂, using forcing = 5.35 × ln(C ÷ C₀).

workedSteps.text: A doubling means C ÷ C₀ = 2, and the natural logarithm of 2 is 0.693.
The forcing is 5.35 times that logarithm.
A doubling therefore adds 3.7 W/m² whatever the starting concentration.

steps.headline: CO₂ rises from 280 ppm to 420 ppm. Find the forcing.

workedSteps.text: The logarithm is taken of the ratio of the new concentration to the old, 420 ÷ 280.
The forcing is 5.35 times that logarithm.

lead.text: A forcing warms the planet until the extra energy lost to space balances it. The equilibrium warming for a doubling of carbon dioxide is called the **climate sensitivity**, and the IPCC's Sixth Assessment Report gives a best estimate of 3 °C, with a likely range of 2.5 to 4 °C. Without feedbacks a doubling would warm the planet by only a little over 1 °C, and the rest of the sensitivity is **feedbacks**: warmer air holds more water vapour, itself a greenhouse gas, and melting ice exposes darker surface that absorbs more sunlight, and both amplify the warming. Clouds are the largest source of uncertainty.

Since every doubling gives the same forcing, it gives the same warming, and the equilibrium warming for a change from C₀ to C is S × log₂(C ÷ C₀), with S the sensitivity in °C per doubling. The number of doublings is log₂ of the ratio, so a rise by a factor of 4 is two doublings.

reveal.text: Each doubling gives the same forcing of 3.7 W/m² and so the same warming, the sensitivity. From 280 to 1,120 ppm is two doublings, which at 3 °C each is 6 °C at equilibrium.
This is an equilibrium value for carbon dioxide alone. The observed warming is smaller because the ocean is still warming up, and aerosols cool.

lead.text: The IPCC reports that the global surface temperature in 2011 to 2020 was 1.09 °C above 1850 to 1900, with a likely range of 0.95 to 1.20 °C. It also assigns that warming to its causes: from 1850 to 1900 up to 2010 to 2019, the likely contribution of well-mixed greenhouse gases is 1.0 to 2.0 °C, other human drivers, mainly aerosols, cooled the planet by 0.0 to 0.8 °C, and natural drivers contributed between −0.1 and +0.1 °C. Together the human causes account for 0.8 to 1.3 °C, with a best estimate of 1.07 °C, about all of the observed warming.

Several independent *fingerprints* point the same way. The lower atmosphere warms while the upper stratosphere cools, which is what more greenhouse gas does and what a brighter Sun would not do. The lower stratosphere cooled too from 1979 to the mid-1990s, but the IPCC puts that mainly down to ozone loss. And the carbon added to the air carries the isotope signature of fossil carbon. The Sun's output has not risen since the 1980s, and orbital changes are far too slow.

afterFigure.text: CO₂ is not the only driver: methane and other gases warm, aerosols cool, and land use and the Sun play smaller roles, but CO₂ is the largest net contributor.
